desc:
Let n be the length of the string s. An operation with value a (positions counted from 1) reverses the substring that starts at position a and ends at position n + 1 - a; in 0-indexed terms, the slice s[a-1 .. n-a]. Such a substring is centred in the middle of the string.

Apply the operations in the given order and return the final string.

s = "abcdef", ops = [1, 2]
result = "fbcdea"

The string goes abcdef → fedcba (reverse positions 1..6) → fbcdea (reverse positions 2..5).
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
1 ≤ ops[j] ≤ (s.length + 1) / 2 (integer division), so every substring is non-empty
hints: Simulating each reversal costs O(n) per operation, and there can be many operations. Look at what a symmetric reversal does to a pair of positions i and n-1-i.
A reversal of s[a-1 .. n-a] swaps every pair (i, n-1-i) with i ≥ a-1 and leaves the outer pairs alone. Pairs never move to a different pair.
Count, for each pair index i, how many operations have a - 1 ≤ i (a prefix count over the operation values). If that count is odd, the pair ends up swapped.
editorial: Reversing a centred segment maps position i to position n-1-i for every position inside the segment. So the characters always stay on their own pair {i, n-1-i}; each operation either swaps the two characters of a pair (if the pair is inside the segment) or does nothing. Two swaps cancel, so only the parity matters.

Pair i (for i < n/2) is inside the segment of operation a exactly when a - 1 ≤ i. Mark each operation at index a-1, sweep i from the left while keeping the XOR of the marks seen so far, and swap the pair when that parity is 1. The middle character of an odd-length string never moves. Time O(n + m), space O(n).
